table.title: The finish dial: scaling 8 RL directions per matrix sets how often the base finishes, and near size 1.5 it matches RL on the 328
table.claim:
Scaling the top 8 singular directions of (RL-Math 3.1 minus base) in each of 224 matrices sets how often base + cue finishes on hard328 (T 1.0, grader v3, one sample per cell).

- **Cap hits** at sizes -1, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3: 96, 77, 50, 46, 25, 5, 9. They fall up to 2x and stay low at 3x.
- **Right:** 118, 164, 170, 192, 203, 190, 117. RL scores 206 with 20 cap hits.
- **Random control:** a matched random rank-8 edit is flat at sizes -1, 1, 2, 3 (158 to 167 right, 67 to 79 cap hits). It was not run at 0.5 or 1.5.
- **Size 1:** top-8 is +10.4 points [5.8, 14.9] over random and still -4.3 [-8.2, -0.3] below RL.
- **Size 1.5:** chosen as the best of 7 sizes on the 328. One sample is -0.9 [-4.9, 2.7] against RL. It now replicates on four new draws of the same problems: 207, 198, 199, 197 (mean 200.25, cap hits 14 to 22) against RL's four-sample mean of 200.0, a difference of +0.1 [-1.7, 1.8]. The vote over 4 is 214 against RL's 221.
- **Held out:** MATH-500 at size 1.5 is 456 of 500, one sample.
- **Noise:** the same-seed rerun differs by 4 problems, so differences of that size between single cells are noise.
- **Rank sweep at size 1:** k=1 181, k=8 192, k=64 200 (-1.8 [-5.5, 1.8] against RL).
- **Other rewards:** the finishing effect holds for the Math and Code checkpoints (Code 3.1 178/41, Code 3.0 173/23, Math 3.0 182/43). It does not hold for every reward: General 3.0 top-8 gives 164/88, no gain and more cap hits than the base; IF cuts cap hits to 41 but scores 155, below the base; Think-SFT top-8 gives 0 of 328.
- **Cascade:** 207 at 11,696 tokens is the best of 8 cut points, is estimated from truncated stored runs, and equals the cascade that uses RL itself as the second pass. It is a tie with RL at 26 % more tokens, not a win.
- **Reward:** the directions come from RL's weights, so reward is used indirectly.
table.artifacts: branch sharedsub (commit b9bd5f3): studies/rlneurons/results/xreward/edits/readout.json (cells top8xm1_math31 ... top8x3_math31) and run folders, results/xreward/lengths-01/readout.json, specs/SPEC_xreward.md; tools/finding_the_finish_dial.py (page /finding/the-finish-dial); board result-6f1bb7, result-ad3c24, result-284db5, result-1b6bf2, result-51a0e7; replication open as work-ab0f72
table.weakest:
The claim "every reward writes finishing" is contradicted by a cell the finding leaves out. In the same readout the General 3.0 top-8 gives 164 right / 88 cap hits, which is more cap hits than the base's 77 and +0.0 points. IF lowers cap hits to 41 but scores 155, below the base's 164 (-2.7 [-7.3, 1.5]). Code 3.0 is not separated from the base (+2.7 [-1.8, 7.3]).

Three smaller weaknesses:
- **Selection of 1.5:** it is the best of 7 sizes on the 328 itself. The four new draws remove the one-sample worry (mean 200.25 against RL's 200.0), but they are on the same problems. The only held-out reading is MATH-500 at 456 of 500, with no paired interval against RL in that folder.
- **Noise:** rerunning the same seed gave 207 right / 20 cap hits against 203 / 25, so single-cell differences of about 4 problems are run-to-run noise. The cap-hit curve is also not monotone at the top (5 at 2x, 9 at 3x).
- **Cascade:** 207 is the best of 8 cut points (neighbours 204 and 201), and the same cascade with RL as the second pass gives the same 207. It is selected and estimated by truncating stored runs.

The random control is still missing at 0.5 and 1.5.
table.prior:
Taken from the team's paper notes and memory, not from a fresh web search (Exa was unavailable, see searches).

1. "You Only Need Minimal RLVR Training: Extrapolating LLMs via Rank-1 Trajectories" (RELEX), 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21468. I read the stored full text at papers/arxiv-2605.21468.txt. Finding 1 and Fig. 2: replacing each trained tensor's RLVR delta with its rank-1 SVD approximation preserves nearly all of the MATH accuracy gain over the base, on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base. The rank-1 coefficient grows linearly with training step and can be extrapolated past the observed window (71.6 vs 71.5 % for full RLVR). Its ablation table has rank 1 at or above rank 5 and rank 10. It cites AlphaRL (rank-1 SVD per checkpoint) and ExPO (delta scaled by a fixed scalar) as earlier work. So "a few top singular directions per matrix of the RL delta carry the gain, and their size can be scaled" is published. It does not measure finishing, cap hits or answer length.

2. "Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL", 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28751. Team notes only (Sec 3.3-3.4, Fig 2, 6, 7, App B.3.1; board knowledge-29fdeb). It sweeps a weight-extrapolation coefficient a over [-2, 3]. Accuracy never rises past a=1; beyond about a=1.5 answers run to the token cap; at a < -1 format errors dominate; smaller models collapse into token exhaustion sooner. So a scalar on a weight direction that changes length, format errors and cap hits is published, but the direction is the full difference between two RL checkpoints, not a top-k part of RL minus base, and the direction of the effect differs: there larger a pushes answers into the cap, here larger size removes cap hits up to 2x.

3. "Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations", 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09382. Team notes only (App. D, Table 8). Multiplying one column of a layer-16 MLP down_proj by -32 at 9B scale cut IFEval truncations from 58 to 2 of 1,920 and tokens by 30 %, with accuracy 91.41 to 93.07 %. So a very small weight edit that removes cap hits and raises the score is published, but the edit is hand-found, not read from an RL delta, and is on instruction following, not math.

Also in the notes: "Reasoning Vectors: Transferring Chain-of-Thought Capabilities via Task Arithmetic", 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01363 (the full RL-minus-SFT vector added to other models transfers reasoning gains); "The Path Not Taken: RLVR Provably Learns Off the Principals", 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08567 (per the team note it argues a top-singular-direction edit is the wrong prior for imitating an RL delta, which the top-8 result partly contradicts); "Linear Dynamics in the RLVR Training of Large Language Models", 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04537 (larger extrapolation coefficient degrades).
table.what_is_new:
The phenomenon is known in two parts: a low-rank part of the RLVR weight delta recovers most of the RL gain (RELEX, AlphaRL), and a scalar on a weight-space direction changes length, format errors and cap hits (2605.28751, 2611.09382). I found no stored paper that joins them or that shows the following.

1. The dose-response is on finishing, not accuracy alone. Cap hits fall monotonically 96, 77, 50, 46, 25, 5 from size -1 to 2 while right per finished answer stays near 0.65. Prior work reports accuracy against the coefficient; none separates "finishes" from "right when finished". The direction is also opposite to 2605.28751, where a coefficient above about 1.5 drives answers into the cap.
2. Extrapolating the top-8 part to 1.5x matches full RL on the hard subset (203 against 206, -0.9 points [-4.9, 2.7]) with an edit of 0.11 % of weight norm. RELEX extrapolates along training time with a fitted coefficient, not a size sweep of the final delta, and reports rank 1 as sufficient; here k=1 gives 181, k=8 192, k=64 200, so higher rank helps on hard problems.
3. The matched-norm random rank-8 control, flat across sizes -1 to 3 (158 to 167 right, 67 to 79 cap hits), and the negative-size result. I found no such control in the stored papers.
4. Redundancy: RL minus its top 8 still scores 190, the same as the top 8 alone at 2x.
5. Cross-reward transfer: the top-8 directions of the Code and instruction-following RL deltas also cut cap hits on math (41, 23, 41), while the imitation-only (Think-SFT) top-8 gives 0 of 328.
6. The cascade (64 directions, cut at 14k tokens, restart with 8 directions at 2x) reaching 207 against RL 206.

Limits on the claim to novelty: one sample and one seed per cell, 1.5 chosen on the test set itself, the random control missing at 0.5 and 1.5, and a single model family. Point 2 against RELEX is the weakest: a reader could call it a replication of "low-rank part of the RL delta is enough" on another model, with the finishing readout as the new measurement.

reasons.reason: A rank-8 edit of about 0.1 % of weight norm gives a signed dose-response on finishing with a flat random control and flat precision, and at 1.5x it matches full RL on four fresh draws (200.25 against 200.0), which recasts the hard-problem RL gain as one scalable stopping direction.

A signed dose-response in weight space on one behaviour (cap hits 96 to 5) with a flat matched random rank-8 control, and the 1.5x point replicated on four new draws to tie RL with a 0.11 % norm edit; 'every reward writes finishing' must be dropped.

A rank-8 edit of 0.11 % of weight norm at 1.5x matches RL's four-sample mean on hard328 (200.25 vs 200.0) with a flat random control, which says the RL gain fits in a tiny adapter and can be extrapolated; it needs RL weights and does not beat RL.

One scalar on a rank-8 edit of about 0.1 % of weight norm dials how often the untrained base finishes, a matched random edit is flat, and size 1.5 replicated on four new draws at RL's level (200.25 against 200.0).

A rank-8 edit of about 0.1 % of weight norm gives a signed dose-response on finishing with a flat random control and brings the untrained base level with RL on four fresh draws (200.25 against 200.0), which is a cheap, legible control knob no prior paper measures this way.

table.title: Delta transplant: Think-SFT + 2 x (RL - base) beats both parents on the 328; the RL delta trades cap hits for commitment with an interior optimum
table.claim: M(a) = Think-SFT + a (RL-Math - base), cue, T 1.0, hard328, grader v3, one sample each unless stated. M(2) scores 231.5 of 328 (seeds 234, 229; the second pre-registered with threshold 222), +6.9 points [4.6, 9.3] over Think-SFT single sample (209.0, 4 samples) and +9.6 [6.9, 12.3] over RL plain (200.0), at about 9,500 tokens per problem. It is below Think-SFT's vote over 4 (241); M(2)'s vote is not measured. a = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: right 209, 220, 231.5, 227, 213; cap hits 94.5, 75, 54, 44, 33 (RL 28.5); right of finished 88.0, 85.8, 83.8, 78.9, 71.5 % (RL 66.2 %). The optimum is interior (a = 4 is 5.6 points [2.6, 8.7] below a = 2), but a = 2 and a = 3 are not separated (+1.4 [-1.2, 4.1]). Gaussian noise at 1.40 times the RL delta's norm: 209 right, 97 cap hits, 0.0 [-2.7, 2.7] (one seed; no other fine-tune delta tested as control). RL delta norm 4.12 against 467.4 (113 times smaller, cosine -0.002). About half of the +22.5 problems come from the 80 problems Think-SFT rarely finishes (5.25 to 15.5, two-sample mean; with the stratum defined on held-out Think-SFT samples about 1 to 4 right becomes 5 to 10) and half from the 82 middle problems (37.75 to 50.5); the 166 always-solved problems stay at 165.5 (166, 165). MATH-500: M(1) 467 of 500, as filed, +1.4 [-0.6, 3.3] over RL, not separated. The coefficient was chosen on the 328; Think-SFT is a trained model; summing an SFT and an RL vector is published for another pair (2605.00610).

table.weakest: The headline compares one sample of M(2) with one sample of the parents, but at equal problem count the strongest baseline already in the repo is Think-SFT's vote over 4 (241 of 328), which is above M(2)'s 231.5; M(2)'s vote is unmeasured, so 'best single-model row' is true only per single sample at about 9,500 tokens. Second: the shape of the dose curve rests on one sample each for a = 1, 3, 4, and a = 2 is not separated from a = 3 (+1.4 [-1.2, 4.1]). Third: the stratum numbers (80 and 166 problems) are selected on the same Think-SFT samples used as their baseline, so they overstate where the gain sits. The noise control is one seed of one norm (isotropic Gaussian per tensor), which rules out 'any small perturbation' but not 'any small fine-tune delta from the same base' (no Code-RL or other donor delta as a matched control). MATH-500 does not separate M(1) from RL.
table.prior:
Verdict rests on the team's stored full-paper notes only; no fresh Exa search could be run (see searches).

1. "Decouple before Integration: Test-time Synthesis of SFT and RLVR Task Vectors", 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00610. Sums an SFT task vector and a GRPO/RLVR task vector on Qwen2.5-Math-7B. Plain summation averages 47.8 on six sets against parents 44.1 (SFT) and 45.5; the full method reaches 49.3. Reports the SFT vector's L2 norm at about 30 times the RLVR vector's and 44.91% sign disagreement. TIES (37.8) and DARE (14.5) do worse. So "SFT + RL delta beats both parents" and "the RL delta is much smaller than the SFT delta" are already published for another pair.

2. "Reasoning Vectors: Transferring Chain-of-Thought Capabilities via Task Arithmetic", 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01363. Adds v = theta_GRPO - theta_SFT to Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B and sweeps the coefficient on GSM8K: 45.1% base, 47.2% at 0.5, 50.0% at 1.0, 48.1% at 1.5 (2.0 tested, number not reported). So a dose curve with an interior optimum for an RL-derived vector is published, with the peak at 1.0 and no gain from extrapolation. Subtracting the vector costs 11.8 points. It has no random or equal-norm control (team note).

3. "GRRR: The Geometry of Reshaping, Rotation, and Routing in Decoder LLM post-training", 2026, arXiv 2609.22146 (id from team notes; not re-fetched). Reports incremental RL step size at 0.004 to 0.17 times the SFT norm, so the small RL update is known geometry.
table.what_is_new:
The phenomenon is known; the following parts are not in the team's notes of the closest papers:

- **Peak at 2x, not 1x.** The optimum sits at a = 2 (231.5 of 328), above a = 1 (220) and replicated by a pre-registered second seed. Reasoning Vectors found degradation above 1.0.
- **Mechanism readout along the dose.** Cap hits fall monotonically (94.5 to 33) while right-of-finished falls (88.0% to 71.5%), which explains the interior optimum as a trade of unfinished answers for commitment. The gain is localised to the 80 problems Think-SFT rarely finishes, with all 166 always-solved problems kept.
- **Matched-norm Gaussian noise control.** It gives 0.0 [-2.7, 2.7]; neither closest paper has one.
- **Setting.** The RL donor was trained from the base with no demonstrations, the SFT parent on other data, and the set is held out from the RL prompts.
- **Geometry numbers.** Norm ratio 113 times and cosine -0.002, against about 30 times in 2605.00610.

The finding's caveat "the dose curve and noise control are new" overstates one point: a coefficient sweep with an interior optimum is published in 2509.01363. It should read "the dose curve past 1x with cap-hit decomposition, and the noise control, are new".

Limits already stated in the finding still apply: the coefficient was chosen on the 328 itself, and MATH-500 does not separate M(1) from RL.

reasons.reason: A training-free weight sum beats both parents with a pre-registered second seed and a noise control, and the dose curve shows cap hits traded for precision; summing SFT and RL vectors is published, and a = 2 is not separated from a = 3.

A delta 113 times smaller than the SFT change moves a model that was never RL-trained by about 7 points, with a pre-registered second seed, a norm-matched noise null and a readable trade of cap hits for precision; summing SFT and RL vectors is itself published.

A training-free weight sum gives the best single-sample row (231.5 of 328 at about 9,500 tokens, +6.9 over Think-SFT, second seed pre-registered, noise control null), usable next week by anyone with the three checkpoints; SFT+RL vector sums are published for another pair and the vote is unmeasured.

Adding twice a delta 113 times smaller than the SFT change beats both parents by 7 to 10 points with a pre-registered second seed and a noise control, though summing SFT and RL vectors is published and the coefficient was chosen on the test set.

A training-free weight sum (Think-SFT + 2x RL delta) beats both parents by 7 to 10 points with a pre-registered second seed and a flat matched-norm noise control, and the peak past 1x with the cap-hit versus precision trade is new and directly usable as a method.

table.title: The no-reward model's lead over RL grows on 136 contest problems published after all weights existed
table.claim:
Think-SFT's lead over RL holds on 136 contest problems first set 2026-02-05 to 2026-11-07, after all three models' weights were uploaded. It is not shown to grow: the lead is +6.1 points on hard328, a different benchmark, and the interval here starts at +7.4.

Setting: T 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, 4 samples, one run per arm, no restarts.

- Vote over 4: Think-SFT + cue 75 (55.1 %), RL plain 57 (41.9 %), base + cue 38 (27.9 %). Think-SFT minus RL is +13.2 points [+7.4, +19.1].
- Tie rule: RL's top answer is tied on 45 problems, so the lead is between +8.1 and +17.6 points depending on the tie rule. It is positive under every rule.
- One sample: 60.0 / 50.5 / 29.5, +7.0 points [+3.1, +11.0].
- Mechanism: the vote lead is about twice the one-sample lead because Think-SFT abstains by hitting the cap. It hits the cap on 248 of 544 samples (RL 84, base 219) and is right in 238 of 296 finished answers (80.4 %); RL is right in 197 of 460 (42.8 %), base in 117 of 325 (36.0 %).
- Think-SFT's vote is 75 against pass@4 77. RL's vote loses 11 of its 68 problems that have a right sample.
- Vote right for one model only: Think-SFT 20, RL 2.
- HMMT Nov (49 problems): 30 against 23.
- Overlap scans: 0 exact, 0 near in 13,314 RL prompts and 2,268,178 Think-SFT rows.

Limits: no RL + cue arm on this set; one sampling setting and one cap; 77 of 136 statements transcribed by a language model; reused older problems cannot be excluded (one was found and dropped). The result rules out the test problems being in training data. It does not rule out every form of contamination.

table.weakest:
The title's "grows" is the weakest part; every number in the claim reproduces.

1. "Grows" compares two different benchmarks and is not tested. The lead is +6.1 points on hard328 (241 against 221) and +13.2 [+7.4, +19.1] here. The interval's lower end sits near the old lead, and the README's own title says "holds".
2. The size of the vote lead depends on the vote rule. The one-sample lead is +7.0. The vote roughly doubles it because Think-SFT abstains by hitting the cap on 45.6 % of samples, and RL has a tied top answer on 45 of 136 problems. Depending on the tie rule the lead is between +8.1 and +17.6 points.
3. There is no prompt-matched RL arm on this set. Think-SFT has the cue, RL is plain, and RL + cue was not run.
4. Each arm is one run at one sampling setting and one cap (16,384).
5. "Removes the contamination explanation" is too strong. The set rules out the test problems being in training data. It does not rule out reused older problems (one was found), and 77 statements are language-model transcriptions, though that subset agrees at +14.3.

table.what_is_new:
My best estimate, which a search must confirm, is new_twist_on_known; I return "unclear" because no search ran.

Likely already known: (1) scoring on contests published after the weights existed as a contamination control (MathArena); (2) RLVR beats its base on AIME 2026 (2605.21468 Table 1); (3) that a model fine-tuned on reasoning traces from a stronger teacher can beat a small-scale RL run from a base is not surprising to the field, since the SFT data carries the teacher's ability.

Likely not published, as far as the stored texts and my memory go: (a) the paired number on this pair, Think-SFT + cue 75 against RL-Zero-Math 57 of 136 on problems from 2026-02 to 2026-11 (+13.2 points [7.4, 19.1], 4-sample vote), with the HMMT November 2026 problems that are eight days old; (b) the error split: Think-SFT fails by hitting the 16,384 cap (45.6 % of samples) and is right in 80.4 % of finished answers, RL finishes and is right in 42.8 %, so the vote reaches 75 of Think-SFT's pass@4 77 while RL's vote loses 11 of 68; (c) the overlap scans against both training sets with positive controls.

Caveat on the claim itself that bears on novelty: "no-reward" describes the training signal only; Think-SFT learned from a stronger model's traces, so a reader will file this under distillation against RL, where the ordering is expected. The cap-hit against wrong-finished-answer split is the part most likely to be new.

reasons.reason: On 136 problems newer than the weights the lead holds under every tie rule, and the 80 % against 43 % finished-answer precision split is a clear new fact about how RL-from-base fails, though an RL + cue arm is missing.

Every number reproduces on problems newer than the weights and the 80 % against 43 % finished-answer precision is a clean readout, but it shows no weight or activation mechanism and has no RL + cue arm.

The +13.2-point vote lead reproduces from rows on 136 post-release contest problems under every tie rule, which makes 'use Think-SFT + cue + vote instead of the RL checkpoint' a usable recommendation, though there is no RL + cue arm and the ordering is probably unsurprising to the field.

On contest problems published after every weight existed, the imitation model wins 75 to 57 with all counts reproducing and the sign surviving every tie rule, and RL's own wrong answers outvote its right ones (65, 71, 70, 65 against gold 70).

The cleanest headline number (+13.2 points on 136 post-weights problems, positive under every tie rule) with a readable mechanism (cap hit as abstention makes the vote nearly pass@4), held back from S by the missing RL + cue arm and unsearched novelty.

table.title: Think-SFT with the cue, trained with no reward, beats RL-Zero-Math on the 328 harder problems, and wins by abstaining
table.claim: On the 328 harder problems (T 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, same seeds, 4 samples, one run), Think-SFT + cue under the plurality vote over 4 scores 241 of 328 (73.5 %) at 40,410 tokens per problem against RL plain 221 (224 after restart; 222 with ties to the shortest) and base + cue 192: +6.1 points [2.7 to 3.0, 9.5] paired, 26 problems won and 6 lost; 235 against 215 without the 6 training-prompt matches. One sample is a marginal lead: 209.0 against 200.0 (+2.7 [0.3, 5.2]) at 1.08x RL's tokens, a tie at equal tokens (191.2 against 191.0), and not ahead on MATH-500. The counts fit an abstention account: Think-SFT hits the cap on 378 of 1,312 samples (RL 114), 88.0 % of its finished answers are right (RL 66.2 %), per sample 37.5 wrong / 81.5 without an answer against RL 119 / 9, and its vote is near pass@4 (241 of 244; RL 221 of 240). Most cap hits cast no vote (55 of the 378 still carry an extracted answer). Two thirds of the vote lead (+14 of +20) is on the 141 problems where at least one Think-SFT sample hit the cap. The lead depends on the cap and tie rule in size (+5.2 to +6.1 points), no control gives RL a matched abstention rule, no vote at cap 32,768 exists, and contamination of the teacher traces is ruled out only for prompt matches; 'beats RL' holds for the vote at this cap, 'wins by abstaining' is supported by counts but not by a control. Sequential-vote tokens per table.md: 30,837 (Think-SFT) and 31,620 (RL with restarts), not 30,904 and 31,326.

table.weakest: The vote lead is partly an artifact of the 16,384 cap acting as an abstention filter, and it is concentrated where Think-SFT does not finish: on the 187 problems where all four Think-SFT samples finish the vote is 180 against 174 (+6), on the other 141 it is 61 against 47 (+14). - Reliability/capability split (4 further base samples): RL 66 % reliability, 25 % cut off, 6 % capability. A random weight change of RL's norm (417 against 410 of 500, +1.4 points [-2.0, 4.8]) gains 42 problems that split 71 % [60, 83] / 17 % / 10 %. 40 of those 42 are among RL's 65.

What clearly separates RL is the counts. RL fixes 65 and loses 12 or 13 depending on the cap-hit rule (net +53 or +52 [39, 66]). The random control fixes 42 and loses 35 (+7). The base-against-base nulls give +8 [-7, 23] and -5 [-18, 8]. Theta 0.5 fixes 53 and loses 11. RL both fixes more and loses fewer.

Known (from memory, unverified): RLVR gains are mostly problems the base model already solves in some samples (pass@k coverage), and single-run differences on MATH-500 carry several points of sampling noise.

What I do not know of in print, and what the finding adds:
1. A null for the decomposition itself. The same per-problem split (reliability 66 % / cut off 25 %, and the six-part taxonomy) is computed for a second sample of the cued base (46 problems) and matches RL's 65 problems in 0 of 10 parts differing. Prior work reports the split for RL only and reads it as a property of RL.
2. A random weight change of RL's norm as the control: it gains 42 problems with the same split (reliability 71 % [60, 83]), 40 of them among RL's 65.

The result is a methodological caution about a known phenomenon, not a new phenomenon, hence new_twist_on_known. Because no literature search could run, 'known' cannot be excluded: a paper that tabulates fixed/lost flips against a same-model resample for RLVR would make point 3 known.

table.title: Theories on trial: agent-written mechanistic theories predict no better than readers with no theory
table.claim: Over six rounds of the theory engine, agent-written mechanistic theories were no nearer the measured number than a no-theory reader and were overconfident. 399 numeric predictions were filed and 370 scored: the theory's centre was nearer than the mean of the two readers in 182, farther in 170, tied in 18 (a coin flip; predictions share targets, so they are not independent, and 151 of them are round-02 forecasts on shared targets). On the 212 predictions with reader intervals (rounds 03-06), the theories' 90 % intervals held the measured value 148 times (70 %) against 177 and 181 for the readers; the summed log score is -45.92 nats, with gains clipped to [-3, 3] and 25 claims at the -3 clip. That total includes one account theory at +35.41 nats (31 of 44 nearer); without it the total is about -81 nats and round 06 is 4 of 14 nearer. Round 03: -25.55 nats over 80 claims; 37 claims with a centre farther than the readers' midpoint sum to -50.25, the other 43 to +24.70; 15 of 21 divergent claims lose, 11 at the clip; theory intervals are a median 0.62 of the readers' width (narrower in 78 of 80). Round 04: 29 of 42 computed, theories inside 18 of 29 against 25 and 24, -17.32 nats. Round 05: 45 of 48 computed, 1 of 13 survived, -25.45. Round 06: 67 of 71 computed, 5 new theories refuted, +22.41 (account-driven). Round 07: 24 of 27, -12.93, no new survivor. No theory stands as of round 07: the round-06 "stands" was withdrawn under engine 7.1, and the graveyard holds 61 entries (about 20 refuted by their own tests in rounds 04-06, 4 lost to a rival). Both sides' base-only intervention in round 07 was predicted at 450 against the best known 454. The round-06 replication matched 54 of 55 recomputed numbers. The two readers are effectively one reader (centres differ by a median 1.8 %), tests after round 03 were chosen by the theories, and scoring rules changed between engine versions, so this is a description of this engine, not a general result about LLM-written theories.

The headline "no better" rests on a coin-flip count, and the "worse" part rests on a scoring choice plus one outlier.
1. Closeness: 182 nearer, 18 ties, so 170 farther. Theories are nearer slightly more often than farther; the count shows no difference, not a loss. 151 of the 370 (41 %) come from round 02, where a forecaster given the theory predicted shared targets, and the same target is predicted by several theories (t37 appears 5+ times), so the 370 are not independent and no interval is given.
2. Log score: the -45.92 nats is dominated by clipped claims. 25 claims in rounds 03-06 sit at the -3 clip (11, 6, 7, 1), about -75 nats; the clip value sets the total. The sign also depends on one theory: the round-06 account alone has +35.41 nats over 44 predictions. Without it rounds 03-06 total about -81.3; with it and its 44 mostly descriptive budget numbers the total halves. Round 06 as a whole is positive (+22.41).
3. Control: the two readers are one reader twice (centres differ by a median 1.8 %), so there is one null, with no estimate of reader-to-reader noise. The tests in rounds 04-07 are chosen by the theories themselves, and scoring rules changed across engine versions 3 to 7.1, so the rounds are not one pooled experiment.
What does hold robustly is overconfidence: intervals a median 0.62 of the readers' width, coverage 148 of 212 (70 %) against 177 and 181 (83 %, 85 %) for nominal 90 % intervals.

table.title: Prefix hand-off: RL's advantage is written into the first half of the answer, not into late checking
table.claim:
Prefix hand-off on MATH-500 stored answers (pool of problems where the base is right in at most 3 of 4 samples; unbiased subset n 155; one sample per prefix, one prefix per problem, T 1.0, cap 16,384 including the prefix).

RL has no measurable advantage in the last quarter of an answer, and about two thirds of its advantage is already in the text of an RL answer by the halfway point. The split between the first quarter and the second is not resolved.

- **Base finishing an RL prefix** recovers 5.2 [-2.6, 12.9] of 12.3 points at 25 %, 8.4 [1.3, 15.5] of 12.9 at 50 % and 9.7 [1.3, 18.1] of 13.5 at 75 % (42 / 65 / 71 %, no interval on the ratio). At 75 %, 43 of the 155 RL prefixes already contain the right answer.
- **RL finishing a base prefix** loses 1.9 [-5.2, 9.0], 6.5 [-0.6, 14.2] and 12.9 [5.8, 20.0] points. RL as finisher therefore still keeps about half its edge from the midpoint of a base answer and none from 75 % (91 against 90 of 155).
- **Wrong base prefixes, biased pool (n 70):** RL finisher minus base finisher is +17.1 [4.3, 30.0] at 25 %, +17.1 [5.7, 28.6] at 50 % (32 against 20) and +5.7 [-2.9, 14.3] at 75 % (21 against 17). On the unbiased 45 the counts are 16 vs 11, 15 vs 9 and 5 vs 8. The effect survives removing cap hits (30 vs 20 of 64 at 50 %).
- **Right base prefixes at 50 %:** both finish 83 of 88.
- **Hypotheses:** "wrong prefixes are poisoned" is refuted (RL rescues 32 of 70 at 50 %), though a wrong prefix still cuts RL from 74 % fresh to 46 %. "Late checking" and "plan in the first quarter" are refuted under the filed rules, but both by intervals that include 0 at this sample size, so they are not excluded.
- **Control:** own-prefix continuation reproduces the stored scores (base 92 / 94 / 90 against 88 of 155; RL 139 / 142 / 139 against 140 of 183). The "20 of 20 at a 100 % cut" control has no committed artifact.
- **Caveats:** the base fails RL prefixes mostly by cap hit (34 of 48 wrong at 50 %), which understates the recovery. The first posted 47 / 81 / 82 % was on the biased pool of 183. Rates are not MATH-500 accuracies.

table.weakest:
The title "written into the first half" is stronger than the unbiased data. The two hand-off directions disagree on where the advantage sits.

- **RL as finisher still keeps half its edge after the midpoint.** On U, RL finishing a base prefix cut at 50 % scores 104 of 155 against base own 94 and RL own 114. It loses 6.5 of 12.9 points, and the interval [-0.6, 14.2] includes 0. The drop comes between 50 % and 75 % (104 to 91).
- **The supported statement is narrower.** There is no RL edge in the last quarter of a base answer (91 against 90 of 155). An RL prefix up to 50 % carries about two thirds of the gap, 8.4 [1.3, 15.5] points, with an interval that nearly reaches 0.
- **The recovery percentages are not distinguishable.** 42, 65 and 71 % are ratios of noisy differences from one sample, with no interval on the ratio. The 25 % and 50 % cuts differ by 7 problems of 155 (100 against 107), so "first half, not first quarter" is not resolved.
- **Two of the three refutations rest on intervals that include 0.** "Plan in the first quarter" and "late checking" were refuted under the filed rule, but at n 155 and n 70 with one sample that is low power, not evidence of absence. The late-checking interval at 75 % reaches +14.3 points.
- **The 75 % recovery is partly trivial.** 52 of 183 RL prefixes at that cut already contain the right answer.
- **The wrong-prefix rescue is on the biased pool.** 25 of the 70 wrong prefixes are problems that are in the pool only because sample 0 was wrong; on U the effect is 15 vs 9 of 45 at 50 %.
- **Cut position is relative to each writer's length.** Wrong base answers are long (about 8,000 tokens in total), so 75 % of a wrong base answer is not the same stage as 75 % of an RL answer.

The push also does some damage at this strength (13 answers end without an answer against 5 unsteered and 3 random), and more at alpha 0.1 (381, 39 without an answer). The headline "+0.5 [-2.2, +3.0]" depends on which baseline is used. The matched baseline (same engine, same seeds, shared sampling noise) scored 430, which gives -3.4 [-6.6, 0.0]; the +0.5 comes from stored samples of a different engine run. The two unsteered seeds differ by 19 problems (430 vs 411), so with one sample per arm the "excludes a gain above 3.0 points" bound is narrower than the real uncertainty: the problem-level bootstrap does not cover the seed-to-seed spread of a single steered run. The safe statement is push = random direction (413 vs 409, +0.8 [-2.6, +4.2]; both 35 of 65 on RL-only problems), not a tight bound against unsteered.

Second: the push is not a clean way to add only Waits. At alpha 0.068 it already derails some answers (13 without an answer against 5 unsteered and 3 random; log-prob drops), and it reaches 8.32, 94 % of RL's 8.81, not the full rate. So a small real benefit of Waits could be cancelled by damage from a constant vector at every position. The bias arm, which damages less (4 without an answer), scored highest of the treated arms (421) but still below same-seed none (-1.8 [-5.2, +1.6]). This supports "this constant push does not help", less so "the Wait habit is not causal".

Third: the filler reading is one reader, 20 per kind, with excerpts at very different depths (median offset 252 vs 6,202 characters). Early Waits being filler and late Waits being corrections may reflect position, not origin. The README says this itself.

Steers along a 'self-reflection' direction (difference of means of residual states before 'wait' vs matched tokens, single layer or several). 2. Base Models Know How to Reason, Thinking Models Learn When (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07364. Steering a base model with 10 category vectors (including backtracking/uncertainty-type categories), gated per token by the RL model, recovers about half of the base-to-RL gap on MATH500 (Qwen2.5-7B 63.9 -> 75.7, Open-Reasoner-Zero-7B 87.6). Norm-matched random vectors and random positions recover about zero or hurt (-28 % / -13 %; -8 % / 28 %). table.title: The reward of an RL run is readable from its weights: top-8 input subspaces overlap by reward family, not across them
table.claim:
Across 224 layer matrices, the top-8 input-side singular subspaces of (model minus base) for seven RL-Zero runs fall into two groups, not one shared subspace and not one per reward. Overlap (random 0.002, base matrix's own top directions 0.04): Math 3.0 with 3.1 0.476, Code 3.0 with 3.1 0.425, Math with Code 0.22 to 0.26; IF with General 0.187; Math with IF 0.026 to 0.034 and Math with General 0.045 to 0.049, at the base-matrix level and below Math 3.1 with Think-SFT 0.109. Mix overlaps every ingredient (IF 0.380, Code 3.0 0.306, General 0.244, Math 0.15 to 0.20). The two release pairs are mutual nearest neighbours (4 of 4 models, 2 families), and already at step 100 (Math 0.442); each pair shares prompts as well as reward, so this does not separate reward from training data. Output-side overlap is 2.7 to 4.9 times lower for Math and Code pairs and no lower for IF and General. X1 holds on average (0.186 against 0.063) in 14 of 21 pairs; X3 Spearman 0.77 at n 6.

In one forward pass of the base over its own 328 hard328 answers (1,572,055 positions), MLP `up` inputs drive Math 3.1's 8 input directions 8.1 to 11.2 times more than a random subspace with the same singular values (Code 3.1 6.3 to 8.9, IF 2.0 to 4.5; attention `q` for Math 5.1 to 8.6). This is against an isotropic null only, and the ratio rises in layers 29 to 31 for all three models, so it does not yet show a trace of generated text: the Think-SFT delta, the top-8 input principal components and non-math text are the missing controls. Result is on branch sharedsub, not main.

table.weakest:
Two problems, the second already raised on the board and still open.

1. The title overstates the table. Math with Code overlap is 0.22 to 0.26, about half the within-family value (0.43 to 0.48) and 6 times the base-matrix null (0.04). The data show two clusters, {Math, Code} and {IF, General} (0.187), with Mix between them, not one cluster per reward. "Readable from the weights" rests on 2 release pairs. Each pair shares reward, training prompts and probably the recipe, so reward is not separated from data. The step-100 table shows the pairing is already present early (Math 3.0 step 100 with Math 3.1 step 100: 0.442), which fits shared prompts as well as shared reward.

2. The drive ratio has no matched control. The null is an isotropic random subspace, and any fine-tune's input directions lie in the span of its training inputs, so they should beat it. Per layer, the ratio rises at layers 29 to 31 for all three models alike (`up`: Math 14.4 and 17.2, Code 12.4 and 14.8, IF 7.5 and 8.8). The trace ran only on math answers from the base, with conditions Math 3.1, Code 3.1, IF and random: no Think-SFT delta, no top-8 input principal components, no non-math text. So "a trace of the text the run generated" is supported only by the ordering Math > Code > IF on one text type.

Smaller: Think-SFT's top-8 hold 3 % of its difference against 12 to 21 % for the RL runs, so RL-against-SFT overlaps do not compare like with like. Bootstrap intervals pool positions, as the finding says.

NOT VERIFIED BY SEARCH: tools/exa.py could not run (see searches). The three works below are cited from memory; the URLs and what each shows were not fetched or re-read in this session and must be checked before being quoted.
1. Task Singular Vectors: Reducing Task Interference in Model Merging (Gargiulo et al., CVPR 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00081. Takes the per-layer SVD of (fine-tuned minus base) matrices, shows they are low rank, and measures the overlap of the top singular vectors between tasks as "singular task interference". This is the same instrument (per-layer top-k singular subspaces of weight deltas, compared across tasks). It is on vision CLIP models with supervised fine-tuning, not RL reward families of an LLM, and as far as I recall it does not report input-side against output-side separately.
2. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (Hu et al., 2021), section 7, https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685. Measures normalised subspace overlap of the top singular directions of the update across ranks and random seeds against a random Gaussian baseline, and shows the update amplifies directions already present in the base W but not its top singular directions. That anticipates both our overlap measure with a random control and our "base's own top directions overlap only 0.037 to 0.042" control.
3. Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models (Mukherjee et al., 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11711. Shows that RL fine-tuning of LLMs updates a small subnetwork whose updates are nearly full rank and that the updated subnetworks overlap across seeds, datasets and RL algorithms far above chance. It is the nearest RL-specific result: RL updates from different runs share structure. It measures parameter-index overlap, not singular subspaces, and does not group by reward family.
Also relevant, in the team's notes: You Only Need Minimal RLVR Training: Extrapolating LLMs via Rank-1 Trajectories (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21468 (papers/arxiv-2605.21468.txt, lines 108 to 215): SVD of the RLVR weight trajectory is dominated by one direction per layer; it is about one run over time, not about overlap between runs. Reasoning Vectors (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01363 (papers/arxiv-2509.01363.json, title only in the notes): RL minus SFT task vector transfers reasoning; no subspace overlap. From memory, also the model-lineage line of work (weight-based model tree recovery, weight-space independence tests) shows that a model's ancestry is readable from its weights, and Narrow Finetuning Leaves Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences (2025) shows the fine-tuning objective is readable from model minus base activation differences.

table.title: The opening cue flips the sign of the temperature effect on the untrained base, so the size of the RL gap is a sampling choice
table.claim: MATH-500 (n 500, grader v3, single draws). Moving from T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 to T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 costs the plain untrained base 19.0 points [-24.8, -13.4] against one T 0.6 run (319 to 224) and 16.2 points against the other (305 to 224), gains the cued base 11.2 points [7.2, 15.2] (354 to 410), and leaves RL flat (464 to 463, -0.2 [-1.8, 1.4]). On hard328: plain 107 to 76 (different seed base), cued 119 to 164 (+13.7 [8.8, 18.9]), RL 204 to 206. More than half of the cued gain is top-p, not temperature: at T 0.6 / top-p 1.0 the cued base scores 371 to 394 over six single draws (mean about 384), and at T 1.0 it scores 405 to 410 at either top-p, so temperature alone adds about 4 to 5 points (one unpaired estimate +6.4 [1.3, 11.5]). RL minus cued base is 22.0 points [18.4, 25.8] at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, about 16 at T 0.6 with the cue at top-p 1.0, and 10.6 [7.4, 13.8] at T 1.0; so the RL gap does depend on sampling settings, but top-p 0.95 at T 0.6 accounts for about half of the 22-to-11 shrink. The opposite sign for the plain base holds only for the joint change of temperature and top-p; a plain T 0.6 / top-p 1.0 cell is missing. The plain base's loss at T 1.0 is largely a format failure: 130 of 500 answers have nothing extracted and 62 of 276 wrong answers are under 50 tokens, continuing the prompt's instruction text. The cue plus T 1.0 takes the base from 224 to 410 with no training (209 problems turn right, 23 turn wrong), closing 78 % of the gap to RL against plain T 1.0 and 63 to 66 % against plain T 0.6 (319 or 305). Cued-base cap hits fall from 119 to 27.

A single cued T 0.6 draw also moves by 16 problems between seeds (378 against 394), which is as large as the corrected effect. table.title: Long answers are where the models differ: over 12,000 tokens Think-SFT is right 68 %, RL 24 %, base 17 %
table.claim:
On hard328 (4 samples, T 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3), among answers that finish between 12,000 tokens and the cap, Think-SFT is right on 135 of 198 (68.2 %), RL on 87 of 356 (24.4 %) and the cued base on 41 of 246 (16.7 %); under 4,000 tokens all three are 88 to 100 %.

Under 12,000 tokens RL has 706 right samples against Think-SFT's 687. Think-SFT's lead of 36 right samples (836 against 800 of 1,312) is entirely at 12,000 tokens and above, counting 14 and 7 right cap hits.

The gap is a property of long answers to hard problems, not of length alone. It is +34 to +37 points inside base strata 0 and 1-2, +22.7 [3.4, 37.9] in stratum 3-4 on about 33 samples each, and not reliable under the leave-one-out stratifier's hardest stratum.

Within a problem, RL's finished answers over 8,000 tokens are right 12.5 points less often than its shorter ones [-20.8, -4.8] (57 problems, mostly 15 of medium difficulty); Think-SFT +1.2 [-4.0, 7.0] (53 problems). Per 1,000 tokens RL -4.0 [-5.4, -2.6], Think-SFT -0.4 [-1.4, 0.6]. The 28 problems with both cells from both models give +10.3 [-3.7, 25.0], which includes zero.

These rates are conditional on finishing. Think-SFT leaves 326 of 1,312 samples unanswered against RL's 36, so its long failures mostly hit the cap while RL's are boxed and counted wrong. At cap 32,768 only 23 of 91 previously capped Think-SFT answers are right.

The supported statement is: at this cap, RL commits to a wrong answer on long attempts where Think-SFT runs out of tokens. "RL cannot sustain a long derivation" and "Think-SFT's accuracy does not decay with length" are not established. Precision is equal up to coverage 0.50 (94.8 against 93.0 %) and Think-SFT leads by +8.8 [6.4, 12.5] at 0.75.

The counts reproduce, but the reading "RL's accuracy decays with length and Think-SFT's does not" is confounded by which samples each model finishes.

- **Selection on finishing.** Think-SFT leaves 326 of 1,312 samples unanswered (986 answered), RL 36 (1,276 answered). A long failing Think-SFT attempt mostly hits the cap and leaves the "finished answered" set; a long failing RL attempt stops and boxes an answer. That alone can give RL a negative within-problem slope and Think-SFT a flat one. The hand read (6 of 10 long wrong RL answers box a number the write-up does not derive) fits this.
- **The 68 % is a survivor rate.** result-c8b994 (cap 32,768) shows 91 of 93 capped Think-SFT answers finish with more tokens and only 23 are right (25 %). Counting capped samples as long attempts at that rate gives roughly 45 % right, not 68 %. This is my estimate from one sample at a different cap, not a measured number.
- **Difficulty is mixed into the headline.** RL's long answers sit on harder problems: 260 of its 356 are on problems the cued base never solves, against 100 of 198 for Think-SFT. Inside strata the gap is 50.0 against 12.7 (base 0), 84.1 against 50.0 (base 1-2), 91.4 against 68.8 (base 3-4, n 35 and 32). Under the leave-one-out stratifier, stratum 0 shows no reliable lead (+6.7 [-0.2, 15.9]).
- **The within-problem "long" slope is thin.** It is carried by 57 RL and 53 Think-SFT problems. RL's drop is concentrated in 15 problems of base stratum 1-2 (-35.4); it is -2.8 [-11.0, 4.8] in stratum 3-4 and -10.7 [-27.8, 0.0] in stratum 0. The cleanest matched test (28 problems) includes zero.
- **Direction of cause.** Within a problem, a wrong path tends to run longer, so length can be a symptom of a failing attempt.
- **Replication.** One training run per model and one set of 4 samples; RL's single-sample score on this set spans 190 to 209.

table.title: RL did not create the habit of boxing an underived answer; it taught the model to stop, and the guesses follow
table.claim:
hard328, 1,312 samples per model, cap 16,384, RL plain against base + cue (prompts differ). The untrained cued base already boxes underived answers: a blind model judge labels 66.2 % [54.6, 77.2] of its long (over 8,000 tokens) finished wrong answers as asserted, against RL's 72.5 % [63.1, 81.3] and Think-SFT's 36.2 % [24.4, 48.6] (80 rows each). RL minus base is +6.2 [-6.7, 19.1], which is not distinguishable from zero and is not shown to be equal.

Per sample, RL emits an asserted wrong answer in 21.1 % [16.9, 25.1], the base in 14.2 % [11.1, 17.4], Think-SFT in 2.7 % [1.6, 3.8]. Of RL minus base, +6.9 [3.1, 10.6], most is RL finishing long and wrong more often: +5.0 [2.9, 7.6] (381 against 281 samples; cap hits 114 against 286). The asserted-share term is +1.8 [-2.0, 5.6], so an added guessing habit of a few points is not excluded.

By length the shares differ: at 8,000 to 12,000 tokens RL asserts in 15/22 wrong answers and the base in 8/25; near the cap it is 43/58 against 45/55. So the base's guessing is concentrated near the cap. RL's asserted long answers are right 17.0 % [9.0, 25.6], derived ones 66.1 % [56.5, 75.2].

The 137-problem split (183 fewer cap hits, 115 more long wrong, 85 more long right) is selected on the base's cap hits and overstates the shift. The judge's "asserted" is wider than a hand read (kappa 0.60 on 30 model-made hand labels; judge B 0.49).

Supported: the behaviour exists without reward, and most of RL's extra guesses come from stopping more often. Not supported as stated: "RL did not create the habit" as an established null, and "the guesses follow" as the whole cause.

table.title: RL acts as a near-linear sum of small changes to almost every neuron: first-order scores predict 0.542 nats, the real copy gives 0.549
table.claim:
Within the MLP part of the RL change (attention and norms left at base), effects on teacher-forced KL(RL || base) are close to additive and diffuse. Setup: 80 stored MATH-500 answers, neurons ranked on 20 + 20 answers by gradient times (RL - base), scored on the held-out half (1,163 / 1,509 decisive positions, base text / RL text).

- Summed first-order scores of all 352,256 MLP neurons predict a 0.542-nat drop and the real copy gives 0.549 of 0.708, on the ranking rows, one split. Predicted and measured drops also agree within about 7 % on 25 other subsets.
- Best 1 % (3,523) by score closes 13.7 / 18.6 % on held-out rows, against 4.2 / 5.8 % by weight-change ranking and 0.7-0.8 / 1.0 % random (2 seeds). Best 10 % closes 33.6 / 48.9 %; all MLP 67.7 / 86.4 %.
- 88 % of neurons have a positive first-order score; the top 1 % hold 19 % of it.
- 610 of the 3,523 are also in the top 1 % by weight change; 381 sit in layer 9 and 302 in layer 31.

This does not show that RL as a whole is a linear sum over neurons. Attention alone closes 48.7 / 68.5 % on the same held-out rows, and MLP + attention + other sum to 121 / 160 % (0.995 vs 0.708 nats on the ranking rows), so the components overlap strongly and the attention change was not attributed. Hypothesis T3 (best 1 % closes at least 30 %) is not met. The measure is distance to RL in teacher-forced KL, not accuracy.

At the level of the whole RL change it is not additive: attention alone closes 48.7 / 68.5 % and MLP alone 67.7 / 86.4 % on held-out rows, 121 / 160 % together with the other tensors. The attention change was never attributed (predicted_drop is null for attn), so "almost every neuron carries RL" leaves out a component that alone closes half or more of the gap.

Smaller limits:
- The 0.542 vs 0.549 check is on the 20 + 20 ranking rows (2,577 decisive positions), one split, with no interval.
- "88 % positive" is a first-order score from 40 answers with no noise floor, so it is not known how many small positive scores are distinguishable from zero.
- Random sets have 2 seeds.
- Everything is teacher-forced KL on stored text, not accuracy.

MATH-500, n 500, one sample, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, plain prompt, cap 16,384, grader v1: base 57.2, RL 92.0 (base cap-hit share 13.8 %; the team's cued base reaches about 81 %, so only about 10 of the 34.8 points are beyond what a prompt cue gives).

An unbiased sparse estimate of the whole MLP delta (DARE, keep probability 0.1 to 3 %, scaled 1/q) gives 85.2 to 86.8 (second draw 87.8), equal to the whole MLP delta (86.4) and 4 to 7 points below RL. GSM8K (n 1,319) at 1 %: top minus DARE -23.7 [-26.5, -21.1].

What this supports: the most-changed neurons are not special, and a random 0.1 % of MLP delta entries rescaled by 1,000 reproduces the MLP-only transplant, including RL's answer format and length.

What it does not support: that RL-specific skill survives 1,000x noise. The 33 to 1,000x figure is squared weight norm of an unbiased estimate, the top-k against DARE contrast is not energy-matched, and the artifact itself leaves "spread or scale" undecided. Sec 4.4, Fig 6-8: randomly dropping the fine-tuning delta and rescaling by 1/(1-p) keeps task accuracy at high drop rates (0.9 and beyond), while magnitude pruning of the delta (keep the largest entries) collapses: 7B models at p=0.7, GSM8K 46.70 to 0.37, HumanEval 21.34 to 3.05. Sec 7, Fig 5: DARE on an RL (RLVR) delta of OLMo-2-1B loses 0.2 / 2.0 / 22 % of the delta's own KL at keep rates 0.5 / 0.1 / 0.01, with a rule that RL deltas (sign leverage about 500) tolerate about 10 % random keep while SFT-like deltas fail. Sec 3: on Olmo-3-7B RL-Zero deltas the effect sits in signs and cross-coordinate structure, not in large-magnitude weights. table.title: One difficulty axis: 36 arms solve MATH-500 problems in the same order, so stacking different methods buys no more than a second sample
table.claim:
On MATH-500 (n = 500, grader v3, T 1.0, one sample per arm except base + cue and RL plain), the oracle union of two different arms is no larger than that of two samples of one arm. 618 different-arm pairs have a mean excess of -0.05 problems (z mean -0.04, sd 0.97) against +0.29 for 12 same-config pairs. The largest pre-named stack excess is +1.86 problems, with an upper bound of 5.1 (1.0 point). Example: theta 0.5 cue (452) + Think-SFT cue (454) has a union of 478, inside the 472 to 479 of two RL samples, with 50 fixed problems in common against 50.7 expected. On hard328, 21 pairs over 7 arms give z mean 0.30.

This supports 'no pair of single-sample arms is complementary by more than about 5 problems on MATH-500'. It does not support 'one difficulty axis' or 'the same order' in general:
- The test cannot see a second axis smaller than 1.5 logits on 30 % of problems.
- The Rasch-plus-bilinear null result (gain -3e-07) comes from a term regularised to zero; a later 2PL fit gained +0.0039 nats per cell held out.
- The claim's own prediction failed: the Think-SFT vote over 4 scored 481 against a predicted 471.5, with above 479 refuting.
- Think-SFT's errors follow a different difficulty profile (contrast -1.54, outside the one-axis range) and it abstains instead of answering wrong, so it gains more from voting than a one-axis arm of equal single-sample accuracy.
- On hard328, 13 problems are solved only by the RL arms, with no null computed.

State it as a bound on cross-arm oracle unions of single samples, with Think-SFT under the vote as a measured exception.

The item-model line is a non-detection by a term shrunk to zero, not evidence of absence. The selected ridge is 10.0, where the bilinear loadings are near 0 (all exactly 0.0 in the 21 cue arms); at ridge 0.3 to 3 the held-out gain is negative. On largely the same matrix the later 2PL fit (result-bf6124) gained +0.0039 nats per cell held out, which is above the 0.0032 the README quotes as the detectable planted effect. 2PL is itself a bilinear term, so the instrument missed structure that exists.

That structure is where the title breaks. Think-SFT has a different difficulty profile (contrast -1.54 against a one-axis range of -0.89 to +0.83) and its 4-sample vote scored 481, above the 479 named as refuting. It abstains through cap hits (29 % on the 328, against 9 % for RL) instead of answering wrong, which a 0/1 single-sample union test cannot see.

Other limits:
- The pairwise test has low power: 1.5 logits on 30 % of problems gives z 0.64.
- 32 of 36 arms are one sample.
- One grader (v3), known to undercount Think-SFT by about 4 per sample.
- The stored Think-SFT vector (454) is 3 to 8 below its re-measurement.
- On hard328 only 7 arms were tested, and the 13 problems solved only by the RL arms have no null.

'Killed a family of GPU runs' therefore rests on a per-pair bound of 5.1 problems, not on a demonstrated single axis.

1) "Wait, Wait, Wait... Why Do Reasoning Models Loop?" (2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12895). Already shows that low temperature / greedy decoding raises looping in reasoning models, that loops are seeded at high-entropy decision points (risk aversion, Prop. 3.1; temporally correlated errors, Sec. 4.1: same top child on 98.7 % of consecutive revisits), and that once a loop starts top-1 probability rises toward 1 (Sec. 5, App. F, Fig. 16), so in-loop positions are low-entropy. This is a two-stage account (uncertain onset, confident continuation) that qualitatively predicts our interaction. It does not run any position-selective temperature, so it has no 2x2 and no additivity test; temperature is called a stopgap and no decoding rule is tested.
2) "Beyond the 80/20 Rule: High-Entropy Minority Tokens Drive Effective Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning" (2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01939). Sec. 3, Fig. 3: Qwen3-8B on AIME24/25, temperature set separately for forking tokens (entropy > 0.672, top 20 %) and the rest. Lowering the forking-token temperature hurts accuracy much more than lowering the other tokens' temperature; high-entropy tokens are connectors such as "wait", "however". This is the same entropy-split temperature grid, but the outcome is accuracy only: no loop or length-cap counts, no interaction analysis.
3) "ReSET: Accurate Latency-Critical NVFP4 Reasoning via Step-Aware Temperature Scaling" (2026, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.13233). App. B.6 Table 7 and Table 3: a T_high x T_low grid by step/token uncertainty on AIME-120 over 5 models; sharpening low-entropy tokens helps accuracy and raising T_high from 0.6 to 0.8-1.0 helps. Again accuracy only, on quantized models; loops are not measured. Also related: "Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models" (2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05693), which shows entropy dropping toward 0 at loop onset, and EDT (2024) entropy-based dynamic temperature.
table.what_is_new: Known: low temperature causes loops; loops start at high-entropy branch points and are then self-reinforcing at low-entropy positions; entropy-split temperature grids exist with accuracy as the outcome; high-entropy positions are discourse words like "Wait". The null on accuracy (neither gate beats plain T 1.0) is a setting-specific number that goes against the direction reported for other models in the 80/20 and ReSET grids, but is not a new phenomenon. table.title: 100 of 352,256 MLP neurons hold the base's loops: zeroing them removes 18 of 19 held-out loops
table.claim: Zeroing 100 of 352,256 MLP neurons of the cued base (Olmo-3 7B, T 0.6), ranked on 34 of its MATH-500 loops by first-order effect on the looping tokens' log-probability, strongly reduces looping but does not eliminate it. Teacher-forced test on the other 34 loops (cut 300 tokens before onset, 1,600 sampled tokens, detector 2): 1 of 34 continuations is flagged as a loop against 19 of 34 unedited and 19 of 34 with 100 layer-matched random neurons (one draw); 1,000 by effect 0 of 34, 1,000 random 15 and 18 of 34; activation ranking 5 and 2 of 34. These are unpaired counts from re-sampled continuations, 26 of the 34 edited continuations hit the 1,600-token limit without finishing, and normal-text loss rises 5.0 % (8.0 % for 1,000). In free MATH-500 generation the same 100 neurons remove about 70 % of loops (22 of 500 left against 71; 18 against 61 on a second seed) and the 1,000 set 85 to 94 % (4 and 9 left); 1,000 random neurons remove none (74 against 71, run-1 set). One model, one setting; no MATH-500 gain under a vote.

MATH-500, n = 500, 4 samples each, T 1.0, top-p 1.0, cap 16,384 tokens, grader v3, one run per model: the cued base has 1,642 right of 2,000 and plain-prompt RL has 1,840, a gap of 198 samples (9.9 points).

With held-out classing, the "0 of the other 3" class holds 14.1 % [5.0, 23.2]. The cell "base 3 of 4, RL 4 of 4" holds 86 problems and 43.4 % [34.8, 53.2] of the gap. Where the base's other three samples are right, it still fails the fourth 7.2 % of the time (1,268 right of 1,366) against RL's 0.9 % (1,354 right). Only 2 problems go from 0/4 to 4/4. pass@4 is 467 against 482.

The homogeneous null is rejected (0.5 problems predicted at base 0 of 4 and 142 in the (3, 4) cell, against 33 and 86 observed), but that shows only that problems differ in difficulty. The split is reproduced by sampling noise alone (F10), so it locates the gap and does not identify what RL changed.

Of the base's 98 wrong samples on its 3-of-4 problems, 13 are no-answer and 8 are cap hits, so not all of that cell is reasoning slips. Answer-statement failures are worth at most about 22 base samples (10 by label-free rules, 31 by gold-aware upper bound), not 52; RL has 0.

This holds for MATH-500 at T 1.0 only. On hard328 the base has no right sample on 26 of the 36 problems RL's vote wins. The pre-registered "new problems" hypothesis is refuted (18.7 % under the 30 % threshold); the reliability hypothesis survives at 58.6 % (share in base k >= 2).

table.title: No label-free selection rule on the untrained weights reaches RL: on the 328 the base never writes the answers
table.claim:
hard328, T 1.0, grader v3, 4 samples, cap 16,384 tokens: no label-free selection rule tested on the cued base reaches RL under the same rule (RL minus base +6.4 to +13.5 points across 10 rules, all intervals above 0; plain vote 221 vs 192, +8.8 [5.2, 12.8]).

The best base rule (vote over 4 after restart, ties to the shortest) ties one RL sample, 199.0 vs 200.0 (-0.3 points [-3.3, 2.5]), at 5.93x [5.60, 6.27] the tokens (55,306 vs 9,437). The best one-sample rule (restart after a cap hit) closes 20 % [13, 29] of the one-sample gap at 1.48x tokens.

The base's 4-sample oracle is 207 (219 after restarts, 220 over all stored draws). That equals one RL sample (207) and is statistically tied with RL's plain vote of 221 (-0.6 points [-4.3, 3.0]); it is not a bound below RL's vote.

Of the 36 problems where RL's vote is right and the base's is wrong, the base has a right sample on 10 (16 of 35 after restarts). On the other 26, 58 of 104 base samples hit the token cap and 44 finished with a wrong answer, so the deficit is part not finishing and part wrong answers; "never writes the answers" holds only for 4 samples at this cap.

MATH-500, 24 rules fixed before scoring: best base rule 454 at 19,697 tokens against one RL sample 460.0 at 4,687 (-1.2 points [-3.0, 0.6], 4.20x); RL leads under all 24 rules; pass@4 467 vs 482. Restarts add +0.9 points to the base vote (predicted at least 2.0) at 1.50x tokens.

Larger sample budgets and a larger cap were not tried.

table.title: Offline signed self-training loses points by teaching the base to doubt, even when the reward is the answer key
table.claim: One LoRA epoch (rank 16, lr 1e-4, no ratio clip or KL) of advantage x mean-token-NLL on the base's own 4 stored samples per MATH-500 problem does not improve the cued base on hard328 (base 164/328, 77 cap hits; one training run, one sample, seed 3000000, grader v3). With the plurality vote as return it scores 140/328, -7.3 points [-11.9, -3.1]. With the grader score as return it scores 155/328, -2.7 [-7.0, 1.5], not distinguishable from the base. Both stop finishing answers: cap hits 178 and 145, almost none of them loops (2 and 1 by line repeat, 1 each by loop_A), and 'Wait' per 1,000 tokens rises from 4.6 to 10.5 and 8.7 (not a composition effect: base cap-hit and finished answers both have 4.6). Positives-only SFT with an update of equal or larger norm (0.005-0.006 relative) leaves cap hits at 74-76 and scores 167/168, so the cap hits come from the negative term, not from update size. On the selected problems that both models finish, accuracy is similar (127 vs 124 of 144; 141 vs 134 of 168). Cosine with RL - base is 0.001 and 0.003, as for positives-only SFT (0.002). The pre-registered instrument check failed (held-out NLL gap wrong minus right fell: P 0.123 -> 0.090, G 0.128 -> 0.072), so the update did not learn to tell right from wrong samples; the result therefore shows that this offline, unclipped whole-sample signed update at this step size damages finishing, and does not test whether a working signed update carries RL's gain. Not run: lr 3e-5 (allowed by the spec), a random-sign control, more seeds, online resampling. Stage 0 numbers (28 %, +49.5 = 9.2/11.2/9.2/21.5, which sum to 51.1) are from a board comment with no committed artifact; theta(0.25) 182 was not found in the control readout (theta0.5 = 190).

table.weakest: The interpretation is stronger than the evidence. (1) The pre-registered instrument check failed: the update did not separate wrong from right samples on new problems, and the spec said that in that case 'the update did nothing and no cell is run'. So the run tests 'unclipped NLL ascent on whole samples at lr 1e-4', not 'the sign of the reward'. It cannot refute that the sign carries RL's gain; the spec's allowed lr 3e-5 rerun was not done. (2) The matched control is imperfect: positives-only SFT used 2 epochs on 455 examples, signed used 1 epoch on 552/600, and there is no arm that ascends NLL on random samples (random sign) to separate 'negative-gradient damage' from 'reward information'. (3) 'Even when the reward is the answer key' rests on G = -2.7 pts with interval [-7.0, 1.5], which includes 0; only the cap-hit rise (77 -> 145) is clear for G. (4) One training run and one sample per arm: P and G share 515 of 552 returns yet differ by 15 problems, so training-run variance is unmeasured and the bootstrap covers problems only. (5) 'Teaching to doubt' is read from one word count; negatives were 63-80 % longer than positives (7,471 vs 4,596 tokens in P; 8,188 vs 4,535 in G) and included all 26/42 cap hits, yet outputs got longer, which fits generic damage as well as learned doubt. (6) 'Accuracy unchanged where both finish' is conditioned on a post-treatment outcome (the problems the damaged model still finishes are the easier ones). (7) The line-repeat loop detector cannot see repetition inside one line: the saved P 'wrong' example (problem 72) is exactly that ('986 + 6 = 359' repeated on one line); loop_A = 1 supports the low loop count, but the read.json detector alone would not.

NO LITERATURE SEARCH WAS RUN (see searches). The three items below are from my memory only: not fetched, not read in this session, URLs and details unverified. Treat them as leads to check, not as citations.

1) Tapered Off-Policy REINFORCE (TOPR), 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14286 (from memory). As I recall it: off-policy REINFORCE on stored LLM samples without importance correction is unstable specifically because of the negative-reward term (pushing down the likelihood of sampled wrong completions is unbounded), while the positive-only term is safe; it proposes tapering the negatives. If that is right, the direction of our result (signed offline loss hurts, positives-only SFT does not) is a known phenomenon.

2) Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084, and "Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?" (SRT), 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21444 (both from memory). As I recall: majority vote / self-consistency over the model's own samples used as the reward with no answer key, but online (GRPO, fresh samples each step), reporting gains on MATH-500-type benchmarks; SRT also reports collapse under prolonged training. If right, vote-as-return is known and is reported to help online, which is the opposite sign of our offline one-epoch cell.

3) "The Surprising Effectiveness of Negative Reinforcement in LLM Reasoning" (NSR), 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01347 (from memory). As I recall: online training that only penalizes wrong samples matches or approaches full RL on math benchmarks. If right, it says penalizing wrong samples is not harmful per se when on-policy, so our loss would be specific to the offline, fixed-sample setting.

Team paper notes: grep of papers/*.json for majority vote, self-consistency, negative advantage, unlikelihood, offline RL, pseudo-label, test-time reinforcement, positive-only matched only arxiv-2605.26172 (ARBITER: majority-vote failures in test-time sampling) and arxiv-2608.17124 (hidden-state selection vs majority voting). It equals the prefilled cue (410; -2.6 [-6.4, 1.2]) and stays below top-8 copied from RL (427; -6.0 [-9.8, -2.0]) and RL (463; -13.2). judges.favorite: F03: it is the only finding where a causal, signed, dose-controlled weight edit with a flat random control reproduces full RL on hard problems and then replicates on fresh draws. It turns "what did RL learn" into "RL mostly learned a low-rank direction that makes the model stop and commit", which F02, F04 and F13 support from independent angles.
judges.next_experiment: Add only the top-8 RL directions (sizes 1, 2, 3, with a matched random rank-8 control) to Think-SFT and score a 4-sample vote on the fresh 136 problems at caps 16,384 and 32,768. If finishing and precision are separable, cap hits should fall from about 45 % towards 20 % while finished-answer precision stays near 80 %, beating both the 75-of-136 vote and the full-delta transplant; it is refuted if precision falls as fast as in F04 (88 to 79 %). Alongside it, run the zero-GPU control from stored rows: let RL abstain in its vote (drop answers over 12,000 tokens or without agreement) to test whether abstention alone explains the Think-SFT lead.
judges.combination: Taken together, the findings split the RL-from-base gain into three parts, none of which is better derivation. F05, F06, F08 and F18 show the plain-prompt gain is mostly an opening, installed in the first 100 steps and writable into one tensor or selectable from the base's own samples. F03 and F13 show the hard-problem gain beyond the cue is mostly a low-rank stop-and-commit direction that cuts cap hits at flat precision and whose extra wrong answers come from finishing more often. F02, F04, F11 and F12 show the imitation model has the complementary profile (about 80 % finished-answer precision, but it does not finish), and that adding the RL delta moves it along the same finishing axis. The larger claim is that finishing and precision are separate, composable axes in weight space, that RL-Zero mainly moves the first, and that base-against-RL accuracy gaps at a fixed token cap and decoding setting (F07, F10, F11) largely measure stopping behaviour.

judges.favorite: F03: it is the only finding with a signed, monotone dose-response on a single named behaviour (finishing) from a rank-8 weight edit, a flat matched random control across the same sizes, and a replication on four fresh draws that ties RL at 0.11 % of weight norm. It also gives everyone else a handle: the same directions can be scaled, removed, transplanted into another model or read out, so it is the result most likely to survive and be built on.
judges.next_experiment: Add only the top-8 singular directions of (RL-Math 3.1 minus base) to Think-SFT + cue at sizes 1, 2, 3 and 4 on hard328, with a matched random rank-8 edit and the Code 3.1 top-8 as controls, and score cap hits, right-of-finished and the vote over 4. If a rank-8 slice reproduces the full delta transplant (about 231 right, cap hits 94 to about 54) while random stays at 209, then the 'stop and commit' controller is a portable low-rank object that works on a model RL never touched; if it behaves like noise, the transplant gain lives in the high-rank remainder and F03's dial is specific to the base. This is about six weight edits with one 328-problem sample each, and the vote arm tests whether it beats the project's best row (241).
judges.combination:
F03 + F04 + F05 + F19 + F16 + F27 together say the RL-Zero change is concentrated in directions but diffuse in neurons. Eight singular directions per matrix are sufficient (F05), dose-controllable (F03) and portable to another model (F04). Yet no neuron subset carries it: top-changed neurons equal random ones (F27), and attribution is near-linear over almost all MLP neurons (F16). The top directions are not necessary on easy problems (F19), though removing them does cost finishing on hard328.

Adding F08, F13 and F18 names what those directions do: they install the opening (reproducible by a one-tensor hand edit and learned in the first 100 RL steps) and then the decision to stop and commit, which trades cap hits for precision. F01 and F02 show the other side of that trade: a model without the commit habit abstains by hitting the cap and wins under a vote.

The larger claim is that most of what RL from the base adds here is a small 'open, then commit' controller in weight space. None of the 30 findings isolates a weight-level component that adds mathematical ability.

judges.favorite: F04: a weight sum with no training (Think-SFT + 2 x (RL - base)) gives 231.5 of 328 single-sample at about 9,500 tokens, +6.9 points over Think-SFT and +9.6 over RL, with a pre-registered second seed (229 against a threshold of 222) and a null noise control. It is the only finding that yields a better model per token than either parent that anyone with the released checkpoints can build next week, and its smooth cap-hit-for-commitment dose curve says how to tune it.
judges.next_experiment: Build Think-SFT + a x top-8(RL - base) per matrix (the 0.1 %-norm rank-8 part from F03) at a = 2 and 3, and score it against full M(2), Think-SFT and RL on the 136 fresh-2026 problems at cap 32,768 with 4 samples, reporting single sample, vote and tokens. If the rank-8 transplant matches M(2) and its vote clears Think-SFT's 75 of 136, the RL contribution ships as a tiny scalable adapter on top of any imitation-trained model; if cap 32,768 erases the gain, the transplant is only buying finishing that more tokens buy anyway.
judges.combination: F03 + F04 + F11 + F13 (with F01/F02) together say competence and stopping are separable and composable in weight space. Imitation (Think-SFT) supplies the competence but fails by not finishing (29 to 46 % cap hits, 23 more problems when the cap doubles). The RL delta is 113 times smaller, nearly orthogonal, and mostly a low-rank 'finish and commit' dial: 8 directions set cap hits monotonically, and RL's extra wrong answers come from stopping more often. Adding that dial to the imitation model trades cap hits for committed answers with an interior optimum (a = 2 to 3). The practical rule: tune the dial to the budget. Keep abstention (low a, vote over samples, where Think-SFT's vote is near pass@4) when you can afford several samples; add commitment (a about 2, or a larger cap) when you can afford one.

judges.favorite: F03, the finish dial. It is a signed dose-response on one behaviour (stopping) with a flat matched random control, its chosen size replicated on four new draws at RL's level, and it gives a control over finishing that is separate from being right.
judges.next_experiment: Build a precision router from rows already committed, with no GPU: keep Think-SFT's answer wherever it finishes (88 % right) and use the answer of M(2) = Think-SFT + 2 x (RL - base) only on the samples where Think-SFT hits the cap, then vote over 4 on hard328. In the same script, give RL the matched abstention rule that F01 lacks by dropping its answers over 12,000 tokens from the vote. If the router clears about 250 of 328, run it on the 136 fresh-2026 problems with the rank-8 dial in place of the full delta and a random rank-8 control.
judges.combination: F03 + F04 + F02 + F13 + F08 together suggest that finishing and being right when finished are two separate quantities, and that RL from the base mostly bought the first. The RL weight change behaves like a low-rank finish direction: it cuts cap hits in the base (F03) and in Think-SFT (F04) while precision stays flat or falls, RL's extra wrong guesses come mainly from stopping more often (F13), and the first 100 steps install an opening the base already writes 18 % of the time (F08, F06). Imitation supplies the precision instead (80 to 88 % of finished answers right against RL's 43 to 66 %, F02), and a single scalar mixes the two, with the best single-sample row at 2x (F04). The bigger claim, which no single finding tests, is that reward taught this model when to commit rather than new mathematics.

judges.favorite: F04: a training-free weight sum that beats both parents by 7 to 10 points on held-out hard problems, with a pre-registered second seed (229 against a threshold of 222) and a flat matched-norm noise control, is something a small team can ship as a method in a week. Its upside at scale is that an RL delta 113 times smaller than the SFT change acts as a portable finishing module for any fine-tune of the same base, though its vote and its score on the fresh 2026 set are still unmeasured.
judges.next_experiment: Add only the top-8 singular directions of (RL-Math minus base), scaled 1x to 3x, to Think-SFT and score a 4-sample vote on the 136 fresh 2026 problems at caps 16,384 and 32,768, against Think-SFT alone, full M(2), a matched random rank-8 edit and RL + cue. This is weight edits plus 544 samples per arm, so it answers within an hour or two. If the rank-8 arm matches M(2) and its vote clears Think-SFT's 75 of 136, the result is a 0.1 %-norm finishing adapter that upgrades an imitation model without any RL run on it.
judges.combination: F01, F02, F11 and F12 say the imitation model is precise but does not finish (80 to 88 % of finished answers right, 29 to 46 % cap hits, and about a quarter of capped answers are correct work cut short). F03 and F13 say the RL change is mostly a finishing and stopping signal that lives in about 8 directions per matrix. F04 shows the two compose in weight space with an interior optimum. Together they suggest precision comes from imitation and finishing from a tiny low-rank RL delta, so the expensive RL run may be replaceable by a rank-8 dial transplanted onto a distilled model, with the vote and cap chosen to use the remaining cap hits as abstentions. F10 and F24 add the caution that any such gain must be scored against a resample null and under a vote, not single-sample taxonomies.
